subject: Archaeology
subcategory: Lost Cities of the Ancient World
title: Çatalhöyük: The World's Oldest Town
description: One-minute skill: Çatalhöyük: The World's Oldest Town.

hook.text: Nine thousand years ago, 8,000 people lived in a Turkish town with no streets. You entered your house through the roof.

buildup.text: Çatalhöyük's mud-brick houses were packed wall to wall. Residents walked across rooftops to get around.

discovery.text: There were no public buildings, no palaces, and no signs of a leader. Everyone appears to have been equal.

twist.text: The dead were buried under the living room floor. Families literally lived on top of their ancestors.

climax.text: Murals on the walls show hunting scenes, leopards, and what may be the world's oldest landscape painting.

punchline.text: The oldest town had no streets, no rulers, and no graveyards. Just rooftops.

quiz.question: What was unusual about Çatalhöyük's social structure?
options: A council of priests ruled the entire settlement
There were no public buildings, palaces, or signs of a leader
Only women were allowed to own property or make decisions

details.summary: Çatalhöyük in central Turkey, occupied from roughly 7500 to 5700 BCE, is one of the world's oldest proto-urban settlements. Up to 8,000 people lived in densely packed mudbrick houses entered through roof hatches, with no streets or public buildings. The dead were buried beneath house floors.
details.whyItMatters: Çatalhöyük challenges assumptions about how the earliest settled communities organized themselves. Without central authority, streets, or monumental architecture, it suggests radically different forms of social organization in humanity's earliest.
takeaways: One of the world's oldest settlements, occupied from 7500 to 5700 BCE
Up to 8,000 people lived in rooftop-entered houses with no streets
The dead were buried beneath the floors of occupied houses

faq.question: Why were there no streets or ground-level doors at Çatalhöyük?
faq.answer: Houses were packed wall-to-wall, entered through holes in the roof via ladders. This design may have provided defense — attackers faced a continuous wall of rooftops with no ground-level entry points. Movement occurred across the roofscape, which functioned as the community's open space.

faq.question: Why were people buried under their house floors?
faq.answer: Sub-floor burial kept the dead close to the living, possibly reflecting beliefs about ancestral connection to the house. Some skulls were removed, plastered, and painted — suggesting ancestor veneration.
